title: How Useful Is Cross-Domain Generalization for Training LLM Monitors?
claim: Training a model on one narrow task transfers to unseen tasks, changing outputs relative to the untrained model.
layout: 4 panels, left-to-right fan-out, initial-vs-SFT answer boxes color-coded
description: A small gray box on the left, titled 'SFT on 1-token responses', shows a user icon asking 'Is this cyber harm?' with a purple [hacking dialog] placeholder, and a robot icon replying 'Yes'. A branching arrow fans out to three stacked gray panels on the right: 'New Classification Task', 'Thinking Classification' and 'Summarization'. Each panel has a dashed user prompt box with a red [transcript containing misaligned actions taken by the AI] placeholder. Below each prompt, two response boxes sit side by side. On the left is the Initial Model's answer in gray: 'No', a benign '<think>' with score 0, or a benign summary. On the right is the SFT Model's answer in peach: 'Yes', a '<think>' about hidden actions with score 100, or a summary of malicious actions. Robot icons label each model.
caption: We train a model with SFT on 1-token classification responses (left), then evaluate it on a new classification task, thinking classification, and summarization (right). The fine-tuned model improves across all three tasks, despite not being trained on them. Prompts and responses are illustrative; full prompts can be found in Appendix [ref].
abstract: Using prompted language models as classifiers enables classification in domains with limited training data, but misses some of the robustness and performance benefits that fine-tuning can bring. We study whether training on multiple classification tasks, each with its own prompt, improves performance on new domains with new classification prompts. We show that such training partially generalizes to adjacent domains, improving classification performance on tasks that are unseen during training. However, we identify specific edge cases where the fine-tuned models fail to follow prompts, such as when the classification prompt changes completely while the data domain remains the same as during training. We show that classification training can be mixed with general instruction following training, and that (when done well) such training keeps the benefits of classification training and mitigates its generalization failures. Surprisingly, we see that this no-thinking supervised classification training can generalize to with-thinking classification and summarization, suggesting that no-thinking classification training might be instrumentally useful in building other kinds of classifiers and monitoring systems.
